subject: Chemistry
title: Sugar and Tooth Decay
description: A short lesson to help you apply Sugar and Tooth Decay.

hook.text: Sugar doesn't directly damage teeth. Bacteria eat sugar and excrete lactic acid—and the acid dissolves enamel.

buildup.text: Streptococcus mutans bacteria form biofilms (plaque) on teeth. They ferment sugar into lactic acid.

discovery.text: Lactic acid lowers pH below 5.5 on the tooth surface. At this point, calcium phosphate in enamel starts dissolving.

twist.text: Saliva naturally buffers pH back to neutral and re-mineralizes enamel. But constant snacking doesn't give it time.

climax.text: Xylitol gum helps because bacteria can't ferment xylitol. They eat it but produce no acid—and eventually starve.

punchline.text: Bacteria eat sugar, excrete acid, enamel dissolves. Cavities are bacterial waste.

quiz.question: How does sugar cause tooth decay?
options: Bacteria ferment sugar into lactic acid that dissolves tooth enamel
Sugar directly reacts with calcium in teeth
Sugar sticks to teeth and physically erodes the surface

details.summary: Tooth decay occurs when oral bacteria, primarily Streptococcus mutans, metabolize sugars and produce lactic acid as a byproduct. This acid dissolves the hydroxyapatite mineral in tooth enamel through demineralization..
details.whyItMatters: Dental caries is the most common chronic disease globally, affecting billions of people. Understanding the chemistry of sugar-mediated acid production guided fluoride treatment and modern preventive dentistry.
takeaways: Bacteria convert sugars to lactic acid that dissolves tooth enamel
Hydroxyapatite mineral dissolves below a critical pH of about 5.5
Fluoride replaces hydroxyl groups in enamel, making it acid-resistant

faq.question: How does fluoride toothpaste actually protect teeth from decay?
faq.answer: Fluoride ions replace hydroxyl groups in hydroxyapatite to form fluorapatite, which is more resistant to acid dissolution. Fluoride also inhibits bacterial enzymes that produce acid and promotes remineralization of early enamel lesions. This triple action makes it highly effective.

faq.question: Why is frequent snacking worse for teeth than eating the same amount of sugar at once?
faq.answer: Each sugar exposure triggers twenty to thirty minutes of acid production that lowers pH below the critical enamel dissolution threshold. Frequent snacking means continuous acid attacks with no recovery time for saliva to remineralize. A single larger exposure causes only one acid cycle.
